newsitem.title: UK: Major sets out to woo back Worcester Woman's vote.
newsitem.headline: Major sets out to woo back Worcester Woman's vote.

text.p: The political marketing experts reckon Britain's election will be decided by Worcester Woman -- and the bad news for Prime Minister John Major is that she seems to be deserting his Conservative Party.

Worcester Woman is handy shorthand for the aspiring middle-class voters in a swathe of marginal English seats who will determine whether the Conservatives win an unprecedented fifth term of office on May 1 or hand over to Tony Blair's Labour Party for the first time since 1979.
On Tuesday Major visited Worcester, an attractive cathedral town that was home to the composer Edward Elgar, to shore up the Conservatives' slender notional majority of just under 3,000.
But, as with other very unscientific straw polls that Reuters has conducted on the campaign trail, the mood appears to be swinging against the ruling party.

While Major was visiting the Royal Worcester porcelain factory, founded in 1751 and one of the world's oldest, 10 of the plant's female tour guides chatted in the spring sunshine about how they would vote.
Some were undecided, but only one said she would definitely vote for the Conservatives. In 1992, four of the 10 backed Major's party and a fifth would have done so if she had not been abroad.

One of the four, Val Hastings, cited Europe and the state of the health service as the main reasons why she planned to desert the Conservatives for either the Referendum Party, which wants a plebiscite on Britain's relations with the European Union, or the minority Liberal Democrats.
"It won't be the Conservatives. I'm just disenchanted with their policies at the moment," Hastings said.
Marie Gadd is also leaning toward the Referendum Party, which is bankrolled by Anglo-French billionaire Sir James Goldsmith.

Gadd said she was not passionately opposed to the Conservatives, for whom she voted in 1992, recognising that the British economy was looking up. And she acknowledged that a vote for the Referendum Party, which is polling just two percent nationwide, would probably be wasted.
But she said: "It seems we're heading toward government from Brussels, and I just want people to know how strongly I feel about that."

A desire to give the Conservatives a bloody nose is tempting some Worcester Women who voted for the Liberal Democrats five years ago to switch to Labour, which needs just a 2.8 percent swing to capture the seat. Labour has a nationwide poll lead of about 20 percentage points.
"I fear if I vote for the Liberals it'll be a wasted vote," said Irene Sands, who said she would back Labour.
Sibyl Hutchings said she was still undecided but was also leaning toward Tony Blair's Labour Party. "I rather think that it's throwing away a vote if you go for the Liberal Democrats," she agreed.
The only declared Conservative voter was Irene Tombs, who said she had been a big fan of Margaret Thatcher and would stay loyal to her successor.
"I'm very sorry she's gone, but I'm afraid of the alternatives," she said.
Jose Morris also admitted to doubts about Blair's party. "People have lots of bad memories of Labour," she said.

But Morris was also unenthusiastic about the Conservatives, for whom she voted in 1992, complaining that the ruling party had become too right-wing. "They don't relate to the ordinary people and to the less well-off," she said.
Major, with more than three weeks to polling day, might be encouraged that several of the Worcester Women, as befits their floating status, are still willing to be swayed by the arguments.
